opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the more interesting design questions for us. When you're building a video model at scale, the naive thing is full attention over every token across space and time, but memory grows quadratically with the number of tokens, and with video that gets out of hand very quickly.

The spatiotemporal Transformer we used factorizes the attention. Within each layer you have a spatial attention block, where tokens attend only to other tokens in the same frame, and then a temporal attention block, where each token attends to the tokens at the same spatial position across previous frames, with causal masking. Compute then scales roughly linearly with the number of frames, which matters a lot when you want to generate long, interactive sequences.

When we compared that against an architecture that handles each frame more independently, which is more or less what a spatial-only ViT-style approach gives you, the per-frame reconstructions could look reasonable. But you lose temporal consistency. Objects flicker, the dynamics don't hold together, and for something like a world model, where the whole point is that actions have consistent consequences over time, that's a real problem.

The factorized spatiotemporal version gave us the best trade-off. It was much cheaper than full spatiotemporal attention, so we could scale it, and it captured the dynamics well enough that the downstream video generation and the learned latent actions were noticeably better. For me, the main lesson was that you don't necessarily need every token talking to every other token. You need the right inductive bias about how space and time relate, and the factorized design gets you most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

r001.rationale: The response says full attention across all space-time tokens is costly and describes temporal attention across previous frames at the same spatial position. It does not attribute SeViT’s cost to attending across multiple frames or contrast that with a Transformer restricting temporal attention to a single token.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this came out of the tokenizer work in Genie. The tokenizer is the piece that takes raw video frames and compresses them into discrete tokens that the rest of the model actually operates on, so the choice there matters a lot for everything downstream.

The simplest thing you can do is tokenize each frame independently with a standard ViT, which is roughly what we mean by the spatial-only baseline. It works, but every frame has to re-encode all of the static stuff, the background, the parts of the scene that aren't changing, and you throw away a lot of the information about how things move between frames. For a model whose whole job is to predict what happens next when an agent takes an action, that felt like the wrong inductive bias.

So we compared that against a spatiotemporal variant, where the tokenizer gets to attend across time as well as within a frame. The way we did it is a factorized attention, so you alternate spatial attention within a frame and temporal attention across frames at the same position, rather than doing full attention over every patch in every frame, which just gets too expensive. And importantly the temporal attention is causal, so a token at time t only sees frames up to t, which is what you want if you're going to generate frames one step at a time later.

What we found was that at a matched parameter budget, the spatiotemporal tokenizer gave us noticeably better reconstructions and better video fidelity scores than the per-frame one. The encoding was just more efficient, because it could spend its capacity on what changed rather than re-describing the same scene over and over. And that improvement carried through to the dynamics model and the latent action model, which both sit on top of those tokens. The latent actions in particular got cleaner, because the tokens already carried some notion of motion, so the model didn't have to rediscover it from scratch.

The one caveat I'd give is that it's not free. The spatiotemporal version is more compute-hungry at training time, and you have to be careful about the causal masking, because if any future information leaks into the tokens, the downstream model can cheat and you get very misleading results. But once we had that right, it was pretty clearly the better choice, and it's what we used for the final model.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the spatiotemporal tokenizer uses temporal attention across frames and is more compute-hungry, but it does not identify SeViT or attribute its high cost to attending across multiple frames compared with a Transformer that restricts temporal attention to a single token.
